4.text: There are, however, as I said before, many shamans, though they have

5.text: many keˊlet at their disposal, whose predictions are wrong, and their advice

6.text: worse than useless, and there are those even to whom the aid of conjury

7.text: and divination is wholly denied. On the other hand, there are shamans who

8.text: claim very little outward communication with the “spirits,” but give magical

9.text: advice as a kind of internal, subjective inspiration, after self-communion for a

10.text: few moments. These, notwithstanding the simplicity of their proceedings,

11.text: usually enjoy the highest consideration of their neighbors.

12.text: For instance, one shaman, by name G̣almuˊurg̣ɪn, whom I met in the

13.text: Anui country, declined to talk openly with “spirits,” and nothing was known

14.text: about his connection with them. The Chukchee said that he was “[with] only

15.text: his [own] body” (em-uviˊkɪlɪn); that is, that no other beings were seen to

16.text: assist him in his actions. When giving a séance, he began by beating the
16.note: good catch; §2.15 withdrawn: printed mark restored, read off the scan

17.text: drum and singing; but in a few minutes he would leave off the exercise, and

18.text: drawing a few long, almost hysterical breaths, would immediately proceed to

19.text: foretell the future. He talked to many people present, one by one. When he

20.text: was through with one case, he would stop for a while, as if recollecting himself,

21.text: and then, after several deep-drawn sighs, would pass on to the next applicant.

22.text: The third category embraces the “producing of incantations” (êwg̣anvaˊ-

23.text: tɪrg̣ɪn), which includes the more complicated practices of shamanism. The

24.text: incantations, together with the spells, form the greater part of Chukchee magic,

25.text: to which I shall devote a special chapter.

26.text: There are incantations both of a benevolent and malevolent character. The

27.text: Chukchee have some idea of the difference between “well-minded” (teñ-čɪˊmñulɪn)

28.text: shamans, who ply their art in order to help the sufferers, and “mischievous”

29.text: (kurg̣-eñeˊñɪlɪt or kuˊñičh-eñeˊñɪlɪt, literally “mocking shamans”) shamans, who

30.text: are bent on doing harm to people.
